<explanation>
1. Identify the project type and purpose
   - This is an open‑source High‑Frequency Trading (HFT) backtesting and live‑trading framework.  
   - Written primarily in Rust as a Cargo workspace with multiple crates:
     • collector – market data fetchers  
     • connector – real‑time exchange connectors and order managers  
     • hftbacktest – core backtest & live‐trade engine  
     • hftbacktest‑derive – procedural macros for user algorithms  
     • py‑hftbacktest – Python‐binding & CLI wrapper  
   - It provides both tick‑by‑tick backtesting and live bot deployment (Binance Futures, Bybit), plus Python/Numba APIs.

2. Analyze the file structure
   - Top‐level workspace (Cargo.toml) aggregates sub‑crates.  
   - collector/ – HTTP clients for various exchanges; transforms and writes raw tick/orderbook data to files or streams.  
   - connector/ – builds real‑time WebSocket REST streams, normalizes market & user‐data messages, manages orders.  
   - hftbacktest/ – core engine: data ingestion, full L2/L3 order book, feed & order latency models, queue‐position simulation, backtest & live modules.  
   - hftbacktest‑derive/ – provides derive macros to embed custom strategies into the Rust engine.  
   - py‑hftbacktest/ – Rust FFI + Python package with Numba support; exposes engine to Python users & CLI.  
   - docs/, examples/ – static site & Jupyter notebooks demonstrating data prep, strategy tutorials, CLI usage, migration guide.

3. Examine the README for additional insights
   - Emphasis on full tick‐by‐tick simulation, customizable latency models, multi‑asset/exchange, Python JIT integration.  
   - Suggests two primary usage modes:
     a. Backtesting via hftbacktest crate (Rust or Python).  
     b. Live trading via connector + core engine.  

4. Designing the system diagram
   a. Main components
      1. External Exchanges & Data Sources (Binance spot/futures, Bybit, Hyperliquid, Tardis, DataBento, etc.)  
      2. Data Collector Crate  
      3. Connector Crate (Real‑time streaming & order management)  
      4. Core Engine Crate (hftbacktest)  
         – Backtest Module  
         – Live Module  
         – Latency & Queue Simulator  
         – Orderbook Reconstruction  
      5. Procedural Macro Crate (hftbacktest‑derive)  
      6. Python Binding & CLI (py‑hftbacktest)  
      7. Storage (Optional: file system or time‐series DB for collected data)  
      8. User Strategy Code (Rust or Python/Numba)  
   b. Relationships & Interactions
      - Data flows from External Exchanges into the Collector (HTTP/WebSocket clients).  
      - Collector writes raw data to Storage or pipes to Connector.  
      - Connector normalizes streams and forwards market & user messages into the Core Engine’s Live Module.  
      - Core Engine’s Backtest Module consumes stored raw data for offline simulation.  
      - Latency & queue simulation modules inside Core Engine sit between message ingestion and order execution logic.  
      - hftbacktest‑derive generates boilerplate to hook User Strategy Code into Engine event loop.  
      - py‑hftbacktest wraps Core Engine API for Python users, invoking Numba‐compiled user strategies.  
      - CLI (py‑hftbacktest) and Rust binaries (examples in each crate) orchestrate end‑to‑end runs.  
   c. Architectural patterns & design principles
      - Modular Rust Cargo workspace: each crate has a single responsibility.  
      - Publisher/Subscriber or stream‑processing for market data.  
      - Layered architecture in Core Engine: ingestion → model → execution → recording.  
      - FFI boundary between Rust core and Python, with Numba JIT for strategy speed.  
      - Derive macros to reduce user boilerplate and embed strategies.  
   d. Key technologies
      - Rust async HTTP & WebSocket libraries for collector & connector.  
      - Procedural macros (syn/quote) in hftbacktest‑derive.  
      - FFI via PyO3/maturin in py‑hftbacktest.  
      - Numba for Python‐level JIT.  
      - L2/L3 orderbook structures (hashmap, B‑tree, ROI vector).  
      - IPC (Iceoryx) for low‑latency live communication in hftbacktest live.  

5. Tailoring guidelines for an open‐source tool
   - Emphasize core functionality: data ingestion → backtest engine → strategy hooks → result recorder.  
   - Show extension points: new exchange in collector/connector, custom latency or fill model, new Numba strategy, macro usage.  
   - Illustrate how Python and Rust layers interact at FFI boundary.  

6. Diagram elements to include
   - Components as labeled boxes (crates, external systems, storage).  
   - Directional arrows:  
     • “Market Data → Collector → Storage”  
     • “Storage → Backtest Module”  
     • “Live Streams → Connector → Live Module”  
     • “User Strategy ↔ Engine Core”  
     • “Engine Core ↔ py‑hftbacktest (Python API)”  
   - Color coding/shapes:  
     • External systems (gray clouds)  
     • Rust crates (blue rectangles)  
     • Python layer (yellow rectangle)  
     • Storage (cylinder icon)  
   - Indicate major data flows: market feed, order requests, execution events, backtest results.  

7. Final tips
   - Be explicit: label each crate with its path and role.  
   - Show the procedural macro crate sitting next to the core engine.  
   - Capture both “Offline Backtest” and “Live Trading” flows side by side.  
   - Highlight extensibility: where to add a new exchange, a new strategy, or a new latency model.  
   - Use consistent arrow directions for data-in and control.  
   - Annotate critical performance boundaries (e.g., Rust core vs Python JIT, IPC channel in live mode).  
   - Keep it detailed; break the Core Engine into submodules if necessary to expose its layered design.  
   - Use a legend for color/shape conventions.
</explanation>
